decoDesc.summary:
Only the first half of this manuscript, the one that contains the Gadla Zamikāʾel ʾAragāwi, has been illustrated. The second half is unillustrated. The style of the miniatures is similar to works produced between the second half of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, which is probably when they were executed. Because of the style of the illuminations, the former owner of this manuscript, Juel-Jensen, believed, with reason, that the note added at a later date to the manuscripts on – which records its donation by two monks and to the newly dedicated monastery of Zamikāʾel ʾAragāwi in Badāwo – references both the reigns of ʾIyāsu I and ʾIyāsu II, that is that the manuscript was produced during the former’s reign but donated to Zamikāʾel ʾAragāwi in Badāwo during the latter’s reign.
The palaeography of the rubricated captions that accompany all the illustrations is similar to that of the main text, indicating that these were executed closely in time and by the same individual. However, it is worth noting that the illuminator did not always leave enough space for the rubricated captions to be added – as is most obvious by looking at the irregular line of writing above the heads of the Nine Saints on . This, in turn, suggests that scribe and illuminator were not the same person. We may thus imagine that the manuscript was first penned by the scribe, who left a series of blank spaces for the miniatures; after these blank areas were filled by the illuminator, the manuscript was returned to the scribe who added the captions within what space was left available to him. The fact that several spaces were left blank by the illuminator, e.g. and , suggests both a lack of coordination between illuminator and the scribe and that in all likelihood the latter originally planned for even more miniatures to be included in the volume that were left out by the artist for unknown reasons.
With regard to these blank spaces, it is likely that the scribe was following an existing exemplar. More specifically, Juel-Jensen believed that MS Aeth. d. 23 was copied at Dabra Dāmmo. Having visited this monastery on November 13, 1993, he was shown a now-lost eighteenth-century copy of the Gadla Zamikāʾel ʾAragāwi in their collection that included the same illustrations in the same places as those in his manuscript, with the exception of the military expeditions of King Kāleb (), as well as additional miniatures. In all likelihood both the copy he was shown and the copy in the Bodleian Libraries were inspired by an earlier and now lost copy of Gadla Zamikāʾel ʾAragāwi that was either produced or commissioned by the abbot of Dabra Dāmmo to commemorate his illustrious predecessor. Some of the miniatures, such as the one on sit awkwardly within the available blank space on the page. This may be an indication of the fact that the illuminator departed from the model the scribe was following.
Because of the loss of this model, and due to the absence of in-depth studies of the iconography of Zamikāʾel ʾAragāwi or, more generally, of the Nine Saints in Ethiopia (but see ), it is not possible to offer a detailed discussion about this manuscript’s relationship to existing illuminated manuscripts devoted to these important figures in Ethiopian Christianity or to ʾAragāwi in particular. Having said that, it is evident that the manuscript draws, at least in part, on more widespread iconographic traditions relating to the Nine Saints. For example, the images that exemplify some of the miracles performed by the Nine Saints after their departure from ʾAksum on in this manuscript adopt the same iconographic variants used to represent these miracles in MS London, British Library Or. 590 , though the latter manuscript features additional scenes, including the one that shows ʾAragāwi using a snake to climb to the top of Dabra Dāmmo that appears in an expanded version on in MS Aeth. d. 23. This manuscript is also rich in interesting details inspired by local costume and practice, such as the book satchel and tābot seemingly carried in a basket on , the scapular worn by ʾAbrǝhā on , the bed on , the prayer-stick on , the veiled manbara tābot on , and the communion before the altar on . The presence of such figures such as Pachomius, Takla Hāymānot, and Yāred (who is rarely represented in manuscripts from this period), is equally noteworthy and aligns with the strategy of the gadl to enhance the standing of ʾAragāwi as a saint and his monastery by associating them to a series of important figures for Ethiopian Christianity.

decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ረገማ፡ ለሃገር፡ አባ፡ አረጋዊ፡ ወየብሰ፡ ዕፀዊሃ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi blesses the plants of a village that had welcomed him making them bud and bear fruit.
decoNote.q: ወለካልዕት፡ ሀገር፡ ዘከመ፡ ባረካ፡ ወኮነ፡ ልምሉማተ፡ ዕፀዊሃ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi exorcises a demon from a man.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ አውፅአ፡ ጋኔነ፡ እምላእለ፡ ብእሲ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi blesses a sick man with his handcross and heals him in front of his father.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ባረከ፡ በትእምርተ፡ መስቀል፡ ወፈወሰ፡ ድውየ።

decoNote.desc: Two scenes: ʾAragāwi arrives at the foot of the mountain called Sequrā with his two disciples; and he climbs the mountain and blesses a loaf of bread on its peak
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ዓርገ፡ ላዕሌሃ፡ ወባረከ፡ ኅብስተ፡ ምስለ፡ አርዳኢሁ።
ዘከመ፡ በጽሐ፡ ታሕተ፡ እግረ፡ ደብር፡ እንተ፡ ስማ፡ ሰቍራ፡ ምስለ፡ ፪ አርዳኢሁ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi and his disciples pray and eat a loaf of blessed bread on the mountain called Məngərgār
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ በጽሐ፡ ኀበ፡ ካልዕ፡ ደብር፡ ዘስሙ፡ ምንግርጋር፡ ወዓርገ፡ ዲቤሁ፡ ወባረከ፡ ኅብስተ፡ ምስለ፡ አርዳኢሁ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi and his disciples eat a loaf of blessed bread on the mountain called Muḥaz.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ዓርገ፡ ኀበ፡ ካልዕ፡ ደብር፡ ወባረከ፡ ኅብስተ፡ ምስለ፡ አርዳኢሁ፡ እምላእለ፡ ውእቱ፡ ደብር፡ ዘስሙ፡ ሙሐዝ።

decoNote.desc: An impression is miraculously left in the spot near Dabra Dāmmo before a lectern where ʾAragāwi’s disciples layed out of his mat and where the saint rested his crosier and his foot.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ በጽሐ፡ ደብረ፡ ዳሞ፡ ወአንበሩ፡ ሎቱ፡ መንጸፈ፡ ዝ፡ አርዳኢሁ፡ ወኮነ፡ ስዕልተ፡ መልዕልተ፡ ኰኵሕ፡ ምስለ፡ አትሮንስ፡ ወበትረ፡ እግሩኒ፡ ከነተ፡ ስዕልተ፡ ህየ።

decoNote.desc: Two scenes: ʾAragāwi holds onto the tail of a horned snake; he ascends the mountain of Dabra Dāmmo, while the Archangel Michael pulls out his sword and remains at his side to prevent it from harming him.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ መጽአ፡ አርዌ፡ ወአኀዘ፡ ዘነቦ።
ዘከመ፡ ዓረጎ፡ ላዕለ፡ ደብር፡ ቅዱስ፡ ሚካኤል፡ እንዘ፡ ይቅውም፡ በየማኑ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi performs mass in a small before a veiled tābot with bread, a chalice, vestments, and a paten brought to him by angels.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ አውረዱ፡ ሎቱ፡ መላእክት፡ ንዋያተ፡ ቤተ፡ መቅድስ፡ ወተወከፈ፡ አባ፡ አረጋዊ።

decoNote.desc: A man asks ʾAragāwi, who is inside a cave, to heal his sick daughter, who waits at the foot of Dabra Dāmmo since she cannot enter the monastery
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ሰአሎ፡ ፩ ብእሲ፡ የሐዩ፡ ወለቶ፡ እንዘ፡ ሀለወት፡ ታሕተ፡ እግረ፡ ድብር።

decoNote.desc: Two scenes: An army general asks ʾAragāwi who is in his cave to heal his daughter; he climbs down Dabra Dāmmo and finds she has been freed from the demon.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ወጽአ፡ እምኔሃ፡ ጋኔነ።

decoNote.desc: Thanks to ʾAragāwi blessing King Kāleb marches unseen by his enemies in an underground passage.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ባረኮ፡ ለካሌብ፡ ንጉሥ፡ ወተርኀወት፡ ሎቱ፡ ምድር።

decoNote.desc: Two scenes: King Kāleb on horseback and his men with shields and spears kill the sorcerer Finḥas and his soldiers in Nāǧrān; and rebuild the destroyed church of this country (the structure in the upper left register of the folio in which the king and his men are placed, which is similar to that found on the previous page, could represent either a tunnel use to reach Nāǧrān or a trench used to reach the newly constructed church).
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ቀተሎ፡ ለፊንሐስ፡ አላዊ፡ ወለኵሉ፡ ሠራዊቱ። ወሐነፀ፡ ቤተ፡ ክርስቲያን፡ ህየ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi, flanked by attendants holdings candles and a chalice, offers the bread of the communion to the King Gabra Masqal and his soldiers (and possibly also the bishop) before a veiled altar in the newly consecrated church of Dabra Dāmmo commissioned by this ruler
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ወረደ፡ ሎቱ፡ መንፈስ፡ ቅዱስ፡ በጊዜ፡ ቍርባን፡ በአምሳለ፡ ርግብ፡ ወተመጠው፡ እምእደዊሁ፡ ቍርባነ፡ ንጉሥ፡ ወሠራዊቱ።
ወዘከመ፡ ሐነፀ፡ ሎቱ፡ ቤተ፡ ክርስቲያን።

decoNote.desc: Jesus Christ grants a Kidān to ʾAragāwi that all that partake from the Eucharist from his hands will be saved.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ወሀቦ፡ ኪዳነ፡ እግዚእነ፡ ኢየሱስ፡ ክርስቶስ፡ ከመ፡ ይሕየው፡ ሎቱ፡ ኵሎሙ፡ እለ፡ ተመጠው፡ ቍርባነ፡ በእዴሁ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi gives his blessing to King Gabra Masqal who kneels before without his crown on his head
decoNote.q: ከመ፡ ባረኮ፡ አባ፡ አረጋዊ፡ ለንጉሥ፡ ገብረ፡ መስቀል።

decoNote.desc: The followers of the king are also blessed.
decoNote.q: ሕዝብኒ፡ ዘከመ፡ ተባረኩ፡ ምስሌሁ።

decoNote.desc: Two scenes: Yāred and ʾAragāwi meet and embrace each other atop Dabra Dāmmo; and Yāred sings before the newly consecrated church that angels will visit it.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ተራከቦ፡ ያሬድ፡ ለአቡነ፡ አራጋዊ፡ ወይቤ፡ ኪያከ፡ መሠረተ፡ አንተ፡ ብነ።
ዘከመ፡ ቦአ፡ ቤተ፡ መቅደስ፡ ወይቤ፡ ይሔውጽዋ፡ መለእክት።

decoNote.desc: The second Kidān between Jesus Christ and ʾAragāwi that grants redemption to those who celebrate his commemoration and invoke his name.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ነስአ፡ ኪዳነ፡ እምኀበ፡ አምላኩ፡ አቡነ፡ አረጋዊ፡ ከመ፡ ይርከቡ፡ ሕይወተ፡ እለ፡ ገብሩ፡ ተዝካሩ፡ ወጸውዑ፡ ስሞ።

decoNote.desc: ʾAragāwi’s disciples are blessed during a communal meal held during his commemoration on the top of Dabra Dāmmo.
decoNote.q: በዕለተ፡ ተዝከሩ፡ ዐባይ፡ ዘከመ፡ ኮነ፡ በረከት፡ በጊዜ፡ ማዕድ።

decoNote.desc: Takla Hāymānot ascends with his wings to Dabra Dāmmo where he meets Yoḥanni, its seventh abbot, who prays with him and gives his the monastic garb and cap.
decoNote.q: ዘከመ፡ ዓርገ፡ ደብረ፡ ዳሞ፡ በክንፍ፡ አባ፡ ተክለ፡ ሃይማኖት፡ ወነሥአ፡ አስኬማ፡ ወቆብዓ፡ እምኀበ፡ አባ፡ ዮሐኒ፡ ዘውእቱ፡ ስብዕ፡ መምህር፡ እምአቡነ፡ አረጋዊ።

item.desc:
Excerpts from , containing sets of antiphons for Palm Sunday (), Good Friday (), Holy Saturday (), and from the , containing sets of antiphons for Easter Sunday and other Easter-related occasions, including the feast of Adam (), for the feasts of Ascension (), Pentecost (), the Transfiguration (), the Assumption of Mary (),
ʾAbbā ʾAragāwi (), Christmas (Lədat, ), and, possibly, the Pact of Mercy (Kidāna məḥrat, ). The text is furnished with musical notation (mələkkət).

Amharic note. It is difficult to understand, although most of the letters are legible. It mentions the names
of several priests (qes), the payment of a sum of money, a date, and
the names of guarantors.
Amharic reconciliation record mentioning many names.

binding.p: The sewing has been substituted with a new one but the boards and the cover have been preserved and are contemporary to the production of the unit of circulation.
binding.decoNote: The book is bound in wooden boards covered with reddish-brown blind-tooled leather. The inner sides of both boards are decorated with textile inlays. The textile has a blue horizontal striped pattern with yellow borders on a red background, decorated with yellow rounded flowers. The manuscript is furnished with a neutral textile chemise and a leather satchel.
The boards are cut to the same size as the bookblock and present both external and internal shallow bevels.

Full reddish-brown leather cover. The turn-ins have been trimmed out and at the corners they form butt mitres. An additional leather patch has been added along the inner margin of the boards to fill the gap between the turn-ins. The portion of leather covering the board attachment sites has been cut and removed to re-sew the manuscript. The cover shows a fine blind-tooled decoration, identical on both sides of the cover. The turn-ins and the edges are also decorated. The decoration consists of seven concentric frames surrounding a central rectangular panel featuring a Latin cross. Frames composed by the repetition of single tools, enclosed between triple straight lines, alternate with empty ones. Double circles are stamped at the intersections of the straight lines. Proceeding from the outer to the inner frame, the repeating decoration motifs are criss-crosses, straight strapwork elements, wavy lines with double circles between them, and again criss-crosses. The cross is formed by X-form motifs between triple straight lines. At the ends of the arms of the cross there are three double circles. Triple straight lines outline the shape of the cross, dividing the area around it in four panels. Triple straight lines decorate also the turn-ins, outlining the their margins. A triple straight line runs along the edges of the boards and is decorated with double circles.

Chainstitch sewing on four sewing stations (two pairs); periodic fold pattern; two Z-plied threads have been used. Between each pair of sewing stations there are two lengths of thread. The ends of the thread are knotted in the last quire.
The spine, together with the endbands, has been removed to resew the manuscript. The small holes close to the head and tail of the quires testify to the former presence of endbands.
The manuscript is provided with a one-piece single-walled satchel. The satchel is equipped with a main flap extending from the back to the front panel to cover the opening of the book compartment.

history.origin: eighteenth century According to Additional note 4 , the manuscript was produced for , whose name is mentioned regularly in supplications (see Varia note 2), during the reign of ʾIyāsu II. It was meant for the church Badāwo ʾAbuna ʾAragāwi, also founded by her.
history.provenance: The manuscript was sold as lot 143, 23 June 1987, in a sale of manuscripts at Sotheby’s that included MS Aeth. b. 6, the Synaxarium with the forged miniatures, where the pieces had export licenses, and was purchased by Alan Thomas on behalf of Juel-Jensen.
history.acquisition: The manuscript entered the Bodleian Libraries as part of the bequest of after his death in 2006.
